transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-04-09
Time: 03:00 PM PDT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jack Morris (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Marta Delgado (Aurora CTO), Liam O'Connor (Lead Eng), Sana Patel (DevOps), Noah Kim (Security)

Auto-summary (may be rough): Walkthrough of SDK quickstarts for Python and TypeScript. Showed sample code for auth (API key env vs SAML/SSO), env setup, and quick demo of streaming responses. Discussed pilot benchmarks and security requirements (SOC2, KMS, data residency). Next steps: send quickstarts, security pack, and pricing.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jack Morris: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jack from Redwood, I'm here with Priya and Diego on the SE side. How's it going, Marta?
[00:07] Marta Delgado: Hey Jack, all good, thanks for setting this up. We wanted a hands-on walkthrough — especially the Python and TypeScript SDKs and how auth/ env works for private deploy.
[00:14] Jack Morris: Great, that's exactly what we're gonna do. High level agenda: quick intros, run through quickstarts in Python and TS, auth options, env setup for hosted vs private, then Q&A and next steps.
[00:24] Priya Kapoor: Quick note: we'll also show a tiny streaming example and some Optimize features — batching and cache tips for payments workloads.
[00:30] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. We're mainly worried about latency at peak and PCI scope for any card data flows.
[00:36] Diego Ramos: Understood. We'll avoid storing any sensitive card data in Redwood by design — typical pattern is tokenized payloads, and we can show KV cache settings to keep context without leaking PII.
[00:45] Sana Patel: Quick question — on private deploy, how do you handle KMS integration? We use AWS KMS + a hardware HSM for key wrapping.
[00:52] Priya Kapoor: You can plug in your KMS or HSM. For our Private offering, the control plane stays on your VPC and keys live in your KMS. There's a short doc we'll share; it covers envelope encryption and rotation.
[01:04] Noah Kim: Also can you confirm audit logs granularity? We need per-request traces for PCI audits.
[01:09] Jack Morris: Yes, we provide audit logs and request-level tracing in Redwood Console; we can surface token-level breakdowns, who called what, and include the model and route. We'll add the SOC2 report and a sample audit log extract.
[01:20] Priya Kapoor: Ok jumping to the quickstart. I'll share my screen — first the Python quickstart. File structure is small: requirements.txt, main.py, .env example. Example code: import redwood; client = redwood.Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) — note this is a placeholder, in the hosted flow you set an API key as an env var.
[01:40] Marta Delgado: Is there an official pip package name? We have org policy about external deps.
[01:44] Priya Kapoor: Yes, it's 'redwood-inference' on PyPI. For TS it's '@redwood-inference/sdk' on npm. We'll include version pins in the quickstart.
[01:52] Priya Kapoor: Python sample (paraphrased):
  response = client.generate(model='redwood-1-small', prompt='Summarize transaction 1234 for merchant X', max_tokens=120)
  print(response.text)

[02:10] Liam O'Connor: The model name is redwood-1-small — we might need lower latency, any recommended models for sub-100ms per token?
[02:16] Diego Ramos: For low-latency you can pick a smaller variant or a quantized model; Dedicated pools with NVL or A100/GPU choices matter. We'll send latency profiles. In practice sub-100ms depends on sequence length and batching.
[02:30] Priya Kapoor: For JS/TS example:
  import Redwood from '@redwood-inference/sdk'
  const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
  const stream = await client.stream.generate({ model: 'redwood-1-small', prompt: '...'} )
  stream.on('data', chunk => console.log(chunk))

[02:50] Sana Patel: How's streaming implemented under the hood? Do you use server-sent events or websockets?
[02:55] Diego Ramos: We support HTTP streaming (chunked transfer), and websocket for heavier integrations — docs list both. The SDK abstracts it, so the same call pattern works for both.
[03:07] Marta Delgado: Auth — we have to use SSO for engineers and rotate keys via our secrets manager. Do you support SAML + scoped API keys?
[03:14] Jack Morris: Yes, SSO via SAML or OIDC for Console/Console login; for programmatic access you can issue scoped API keys with granular scopes and TTL. Those keys can be minted via our control plane or integrated with your SSO for just-in-time issuance.
[03:28] Noah Kim: Do the scoped keys restrict model access and network egress?
[03:32] Priya Kapoor: Keys can be scoped by model, route, and even allowed IP ranges if you use Private deployment with VPC endpoints. We'll share an example policy.
[03:41] Liam O'Connor: Environment setup for Private — do we need outbound internet for model updates? Our environment is air-gapped.
[03:46] Diego Ramos: For air-gapped on-prem, we provide an offline installer and local model bundles. For Private with VPC but internet allowed, the control plane can be customer-managed or we can push updates through your proxy — there's a checklist we'll send.
[03:59] Priya Kapoor: Back to code — important env vars: REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_BASE_URL (for Private), REDWOOD_PROJECT_ID. We show a .env.example in the repo.
[04:10] Priya Kapoor: Also an example docker-compose for local dev that sets the env and forwards telemetry (optional).
[04:16] Sana Patel: Do SDKs collect telemetry by default? We require explicit opt-in.
[04:20] Jack Morris: Telemetry is off by default; there's an opt-in flag. For Private you can route stats to your internal metrics.
[04:28] Priya Kapoor: Now a short demo of function calling and structured output. We'll call a 'parse_payment' function and show JSON schema enforcement.
[04:35] Diego Ramos: The SDK includes help with schema validation so you can get structured outputs for downstream processors.
[04:40] Liam O'Connor: That helps reduce parsing work. Good.
[04:45] Priya Kapoor: Discussing Optimize — batching and KV caching. For payments, prefix caching for user sessions reduces tokens and latency. We can show a config: batch_window_ms, max_batch_size, and cache_ttl_seconds.
[04:58] Marta Delgado: Are cache entries encrypted at rest?
[05:01] Priya Kapoor: Yes, cache entries respect KMS encryption in Private, and in Hosted we use envelope encryption. We'll include details.
[05:08] Noah Kim: What about retention and purging? We need the ability to purge specific traces.
[05:12] Diego Ramos: You can configure retention windows and have on-demand purge APIs. We'll surface that in the security pack.
[05:21] Jack Morris: Quick aside on pricing for Dedicated — it's reserved GPU pools. We can give a ballpark after you share expected QPS and seq lengths.
[05:30] Liam O'Connor: We're looking at 200 RPS peak for small text generation (prompts ~200 tokens) across a multi-tenant setup.
[05:37] Priya Kapoor: Great, that'll inform whether Dedicated makes sense or reserved burst capacity on Hosted. We'll model cost and latency tradeoffs.
[05:45] Marta Delgado: For the quickstart, can you show local test harness to run a small load test?
[05:49] Priya Kapoor: Yes, the repo includes a minimal script that hits the SDK with configurable concurrency. We'll point to a Docker-based run for reproducibility.
[05:58] Diego Ramos: Note: when running load tests, use a test model and respect rate limits; we'll provide a sandbox key for your pilot.
[06:06] Sana Patel: Sandbox keys — are they equivalent to prod in behavior? We need the same latency and batching characteristics.
[06:11] Jack Morris: Behaviors match, but prod capacity differs. For accurate benchmarking we'll provision a short Dedicated window or simulate via our benchmarking lanes.
[06:20] Noah Kim: Any known limitations with multi-region routing? We need EU data residency and failover to US for DR.
[06:25] Priya Kapoor: You can pin data region; routing policies support region preference and automatic failover. For Private, you can deploy control plane regionally.
[06:33] Liam O'Connor: On SDK security — do you support mTLS to the endpoint?
[06:37] Diego Ramos: Yes, mTLS available for Private endpoints; for hosted we recommend IP allowlists and scoped keys, but mTLS is available in Dedicated/private setups.
[06:46] Priya Kapoor: Back to a short live example — I'm running the Python quickstart, creating a client, calling generate with streaming, then showing how to handle partial chunks and finalize.
[06:57] [screen share stumbles, small pause]
[07:02] Priya Kapoor: Apologies, small terminal copy/paste glitch — but code is in the repo.
[07:06] Marta Delgado: No worries. Could you share the link to repo in chat?
[07:09] Jack Morris: Yes, I'll drop links after the call.
[07:12] Priya Kapoor: Now a quick look at error handling patterns: 429 vs 5xx vs model fallback. SDK can implement automatic retries with exponential backoff and model fallback to a lower-cost variant.
[07:23] Liam O'Connor: Model fallback is interesting. If we have latency SLO, automatic fallback helps keep app responsive.
[07:28] Diego Ramos: Exactly — you can set policy to fallback to a quantized variant or a smaller model if latency thresholds are exceeded.
[07:35] Jack Morris: We're getting into some live questions — Noah, any other security items?
[07:38] Noah Kim: Can you do a SOC 2 in-scope demo or provide a checklist we can send to our compliance team?
[07:44] Jack Morris: Yes, will send SOC2 report and a compliance checklist. Also we'll provide sample audit log extracts.
[07:50] Marta Delgado: Ok great, let's talk pilot timeline. We want to kick off next week if possible.
[07:55] Jack Morris: We can aim for a 2-week pilot: week 1 sandbox integration + basic benchmark, week 2 focused Dedicated window if needed. Does that align?
[08:02] Liam O'Connor: Yes, pending internal approvals. We'll confirm dates by Monday.
[08:07] Priya Kapoor: Recap of deliverables: quickstart repos (Python/TS), .env.example and docker-compose, security docs including SOC2 and KMS/HSM notes, sandbox key and benchmark plan, and preliminary Dedicated pricing.
[08:20] Jack Morris: Any final questions?
[08:23] Sana Patel: One more — for function calling and structured outputs, can we restrict which functions a model can call? We need to limit to a safe list.
[08:29] Diego Ramos: Yes, function access can be whitelisted per route and model. We'll show config examples.
[08:35] Marta Delgado: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[08:38] Jack Morris: Thanks — we'll send the links and docs. Meeting notes and action items in the chat.
[08:42] [call end]
